title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people the right way, say your name and where you're from, ask how someone is, and see why the Uzbek word for "is/am/are" sticks to the end of a word instead of standing alone.
bekal: greet people with *assalomu alaykum*, *salom*, and *xayrli tong*, each in the right situation
say your name and nationality with the ending *-man*, and ask about them with *-misiz*
build third-person sentences with no verb at all — just like Russian or Arabic

dialogs.title: Dialog — Toshkentda birinchi kun
dialogs.intro: First day in Tashkent. Budi, a student from Jakarta, is sitting next to a young woman in the university waiting room.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: My name is Nilufar. What's your name?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: My name is Budi. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: I'm glad too. How are you?

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: I'm fine too. Are you Uzbek?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Yoʻq, men oʻzbek emasman. Men indoneziyalikman.
lines.id: No, I'm not Uzbek. I'm Indonesian.
lines.literal: no, I Uzbek not-I-am. I Indonesia-from-I-am.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Voy, juda qiziq! U ham indoneziyalikmi?
lines.id: Oh, how interesting! Is she Indonesian too?
lines.literal: oh, very interesting! she also Indonesia-from-?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ha, u mening doʻstim. Uning ismi Rina.
lines.id: Yes, she's my friend. Her name is Rina.
lines.literal: yes, she my friend-my. her name-her Rina.

notes: **Assalomu alaykum works all day long.** It's the Arabic greeting "peace be upon you", used across the Muslim world, and it sounds almost the same in Uzbekistan. It's the safest greeting for anyone, at any time, anywhere — and the reply is always the same: *vaalaykum assalom*. Among friends your own age, a simple *salom* is enough.

**Ismingiz nima? literally means "name-your what?".** There's no word for "who" in it. Uzbek asks *nima* (what) about a name, exactly like English *what is your name*. To answer, *Ismim Budi* is enough — two words, no "is".

**Emas is the only way to say "not" with a noun.** *Men oʻzbek emasman* = "I Uzbek not-I-am". Notice that the ending *-man* moves onto *emas* instead of staying on the noun. You'll use this pattern hundreds of times.

**Siz-chi? means "what about you?".** The ending *-chi* bounces the same question back to the other person without repeating the sentence. *Men yaxshiman. Siz-chi?* A tiny piece that makes your conversation sound alive right away.
**No he or she.** *U* means "he", "she", or "it" — whatever the gender. Uzbek has no *he/she* split, no articles (no *a* or *the*), and no adjectives that change form. That's a lot less to learn.

grammars.title: The predicate ending — an "am/is/are" stuck on the end
body: Uzbek has no separate word for "am/is/are". Instead, a short ending is attached to the last word of the sentence. Learn these six rows now; you'll use them in every unit after this one.
after: The third row is empty on purpose: **"he/she is" has no ending at all**. *U talaba* = "He/She is a student" — two words, period. Russian and Arabic work the same way; English speakers just need to get used to leaving the verb out.

*Men*, *sen*, *biz*, and *siz* can be dropped, because the ending already tells you who it is: *Yaxshiman* can only mean "I'm fine". Use the pronoun when you want **emphasis**: *Men yaxshiman* = "Me, I'm fine".

⚠️ *Siz* means "you" (polite) **and** "you all". *Sen* is only for close friends, younger siblings, and small children. When in doubt, use *siz* — in Uzbekistan, saying *sen* to someone you've just met feels like slapping a stranger on the back.

grammars.title: Asking with -mi, negating with emas
body: Two basic tools. Both work the same way: they slip in between the noun and the person ending.

head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: Yes, I'm a student. / No, I'm not.

after: The order never changes: **noun + -mi + person ending**. So *oʻzbek* + *-mi* + *-siz* → *oʻzbekmisiz*. It looks long on paper, but you say it in one breath.
For *u* and *ular*, which have no ending, the question stops at *-mi*: *U oʻzbekmi?* — that's already a full sentence.
⚠️ *Yoʻq* means "no" as an answer and "there isn't" inside a sentence. It is **not** used to negate a noun; that's what *emas* is for.

blocks.text: These ten phrases aren't grammar to study — they're your emergency kit. Learn them whole now and work out how they're built later.

head: Oʻzbekcha
Say it
English
rows: Please, go ahead; here you are

blocks.text: *Marhamat* is the most versatile word on this page. It means "please, have a seat" when offering a chair, "here you are" when handing something over, and "come on in" when inviting someone into the house. If you could learn only one word from this unit, make it this one.

⚠️ *Rahmat* comes from the Arabic word for "mercy", but in Uzbekistan it means **thank you**, and you'll say it fifty times a day. It's also a common man's name, so don't be surprised if someone introduces himself as Rahmat.

sections.title: Greetings by time of day and politeness

blocks.text: Uzbek sorts greetings along two lines at once: what time it is, and how close you are to the person. This table covers both.

head: Oʻzbekcha
Say it
When to use it
rows: The safest greeting — all day, to anyone
Hi — casual, to friends your own age
Good night — only when parting for bed
See you — literally "until we see each other"

blocks.text: Look at *xayrli*: this one word means "bringing good", and it's used for all four times of day. It comes from the Arabic *khayr* ("good"), the same root as in the Arabic name *Khairi*.

One habit worth copying: in Uzbekistan the **younger person greets first**, and **whoever enters a room greets those already inside**. In a lift, a waiting room, a small office — saying *assalomu alaykum* to strangers is normal, and staying silent feels cold.

When greeting someone much older, people often add a respectful title: *aka* (to a man, literally "older brother"), *opa* (to a woman), *amaki* or *ota* (to an older man). It's not a name but a form of address — a bit like "sir" or "ma'am", only far more common.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the right predicate ending (-man, -san, -miz, -siz, -lar, or none).
Turn into a question with -mi, then answer in the negative with emas. Write both.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Assalomu alaykum! Ismingiz nima? — Ismim Budi. — Men indoneziyalikman. — Qalaysiz? — Rahmat, yaxshiman. — Siz oʻzbekmisiz?
talabaman — oʻqituvchisiz — oʻzbek — doʻstmiz — yaxshisan — talabalar

Ismim Budi. — Men oʻzbek emasman. — Ismingiz nima? — Men ham xursandman. — U mening doʻstim.
